questions.q: What does the abbreviation XML stand for?
questions.explain: XML stands for "extensible markup language", a language designed for storing and transporting data using a tree-like structure of tags.

questions.q: Unlike HTML, XML does not use predefined tags, so tags can be given names that describe the data.
questions.explain: This flexibility is a defining feature of XML compared with HTML's fixed tag set.

questions.q: In XML, what characters do the built-in entities < and > represent?
choices: < and >
( and )
{ and }
[ and ]
questions.explain: < and > stand for the metacharacters < and > that denote XML tags, so they must be represented as entities when they appear within data.

questions.q: Where is the document type definition (DTD) declared in an XML document?
choices: In the optional DOCTYPE element at the start of the document
In the XML declaration <?xml ... ?>
In the root element's attributes
In a separate JSON schema file
questions.explain: The DTD is declared within the optional DOCTYPE element at the start of the XML document; it can be internal, external, or a hybrid.

questions.q: Which keyword is used in the declaration of an XML external entity to indicate its value should be loaded from a URL?
questions.explain: The declaration of an external entity uses the SYSTEM keyword followed by a URL from which the entity value is loaded.

questions.q: An external entity can be loaded from a local file by using the file:// protocol in its URL.
questions.explain: For example <!ENTITY ext SYSTEM "file:///path/to/file"> loads the entity value from a file on disk.

questions.q: What distinguishes an XML external entity from an ordinary custom entity?
choices: Its defined value is loaded from outside the DTD, e.g. a file path or URL
It can only contain numeric data
It is built in to the XML specification
It can only be referenced inside HTML
questions.explain: External entities are custom entities whose value is located outside the DTD where they are declared, which is what makes them interesting for attacks.

questions.q: Which of the following are valid forms a DTD can take according to the material?
choices: Fully self-contained within the document (internal DTD)
Loaded from elsewhere (external DTD)
A hybrid of internal and external
Stored only inside a JSON file
questions.explain: The DTD can be internal, external, or a hybrid of the two; it is not defined in JSON.

questions.q: What does the abbreviation XXE stand for?
questions.explain: XXE is XML external entity injection, a vulnerability that lets an attacker interfere with an application's processing of XML data.

questions.q: To retrieve an arbitrary file via XXE, how many modifications must you make to the submitted XML (define an external entity, and use it in a returned value)?
questions.explain: You introduce/edit a DOCTYPE defining an external entity for the file path, and edit a returned data value to reference that entity.

questions.q: Which well-known file is commonly targeted to demonstrate XXE file retrieval on a Linux server?
choices: /etc/passwd
/var/log/syslog
/home/index.html
/tmp/session
questions.explain: /etc/passwd is the classic well-known OS file used to prove file retrieval, as its contents appear in the response.

questions.q: Besides retrieving files, XXE can be leveraged to perform server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks.
questions.explain: By defining an external entity with a URL to a back-end system, XXE can induce the server to make requests, i.e. SSRF.

questions.q: In an XXE-based SSRF attack, what determines whether you get two-way interaction (seeing the back-end response) versus only blind SSRF?
choices: Whether the defined entity is used in a data value that is returned in the response
Whether the target uses HTTPS
Whether the file is larger than 1MB
Whether the parser is written in Java
questions.explain: If the entity is used in a value returned in the response you can read the back-end response; otherwise the SSRF is blind.

questions.q: When testing systematically for XXE, you generally need to test each data node in the XML individually to see whether your defined entity appears in the response.
questions.explain: Real requests often contain many data values, any one of which might be reflected, so each node should be tested.

questions.q: Why would an attacker use an XInclude attack instead of a classic XXE attack?
choices: They control only a single data item placed into a server-side XML document and cannot define or modify a DOCTYPE
XInclude is faster to type
Classic XXE only works against JSON APIs
XInclude bypasses TLS encryption
questions.explain: When client data is embedded into a server-side XML document (e.g. a SOAP request) you can't control the DOCTYPE, but an XInclude can be placed in any data value.

questions.q: Which image format uses XML and can therefore reach hidden XXE attack surface via file upload?
choices: SVG
PNG
JPEG
GIF
questions.explain: SVG is an XML-based image format; an image library that supports SVG can be fed a malicious SVG even when PNG/JPEG is expected.

questions.q: If a site expects application/x-www-form-urlencoded but tolerates and parses an XML message body, you may reach hidden XXE surface simply by reformatting the request to use XML.
questions.explain: Some sites tolerate a text/xml body; if they parse it as XML, reformatting the request exposes the XXE surface.

questions.q: Which of the following are examples of hidden XXE attack surface described in the material?
choices: XInclude attacks
XXE via file upload (e.g. SVG, DOCX)
XXE via a modified content type
Entities defined in a JSON request body
questions.explain: The three described hidden surfaces are XInclude, file upload of XML-based formats, and reformatting requests to XML; JSON bodies do not define XML entities.

questions.q: In a blind XXE vulnerability, the application does not return the values of defined external entities in its responses.
questions.explain: Because values are not reflected, direct file retrieval is not possible and more advanced techniques are required.

questions.q: How many broad ways to find and exploit blind XXE does the material describe (out-of-band interactions, and triggering error messages)?
questions.explain: Either trigger out-of-band network interactions (optionally exfiltrating data) or trigger XML parsing errors whose messages contain sensitive data.

questions.q: What character prefixes the name when declaring and referencing an XML parameter entity?
choices: % (percent)
& (ampersand)
# (hash)
$ (dollar)
questions.explain: Parameter entities are declared with a percent sign before the name and referenced with %name; (vs &name; for regular entities).

questions.q: XML parameter entities can only be referenced elsewhere within the DTD.
questions.explain: Parameter entities are a special kind of entity usable only within the DTD, which is why they help when regular entities are blocked.

questions.q: For out-of-band data exfiltration via blind XXE, where does the attacker host the malicious DTD?
choices: On a web server the attacker controls, invoked as an external DTD from the in-band payload
Inside the server's /etc/passwd file
In the victim's browser cache
In the application's internal DTD
questions.explain: The attacker serves the malicious DTD from their own server (e.g. http://web-attacker.com/malicious.dtd) and loads it via a parameter entity in the submitted payload.

questions.q: In error-based blind XXE, how is sensitive data disclosed?
choices: By triggering an XML parsing error whose message contains the data (e.g. a nonexistent filename built from the file's contents)
By emailing the file to the attacker
By writing the file to the server access log
By rendering the file as an image
questions.explain: A malicious DTD loads a nonexistent file whose name embeds the target file's contents, so the FileNotFound error message leaks the data.

questions.q: Why does the error-based technique normally require an external DTD rather than a fully internal one?
choices: Using a parameter entity within another parameter entity's definition is permitted in external DTDs but not internal ones
Internal DTDs cannot contain any entities at all
External DTDs always load faster
Internal DTDs are encrypted by the parser
questions.explain: The XML spec forbids referencing a parameter entity inside another parameter entity's definition in an internal DTD, though many parsers allow it in external DTDs.

questions.q: How does the 'repurposing a local DTD' technique work when out-of-band connections are blocked?
choices: It loads an existing DTD file on the server's filesystem and redefines one of its entities to trigger an error containing sensitive data
It uploads a brand-new DTD over FTP
It brute-forces the administrator password
It disables the XML parser remotely
questions.explain: A hybrid DTD invokes a local DTD file and redefines an entity it declares; redefining an external entity from the internal subset relaxes the parameter-entity restriction, enabling an error-based leak.

questions.q: You can enumerate which local DTD files exist on the server because the application returns the XML parser's error messages when you try to load them.
questions.explain: Attempting to load a missing file causes an error; a present file (e.g. /usr/share/yelp/dtd/docbookx.dtd on GNOME systems) does not, letting you locate a file to repurpose.

questions.q: The material notes that newline characters (as in /etc/passwd) can break out-of-band exfiltration. What workarounds does it suggest?
choices: Use the FTP protocol instead of HTTP, or target a file without newlines such as /etc/hostname
Base64-encode the entire filesystem
Switch from HTTP to HTTPS
Split the file using client-side JavaScript
questions.explain: Some parsers validate URL characters, so FTP may work instead of HTTP; otherwise target a single-line file like /etc/hostname.

questions.q: What is the easiest and most effective way to prevent XXE attacks?
choices: Disable the dangerous XML parser features the application does not need (external entity resolution and XInclude)
Rename all XML files to use a .json extension
Add a CAPTCHA to every form
Block inbound traffic on port 80
questions.explain: Virtually all XXE arises from unneeded parser features; disabling external entity resolution and XInclude via configuration removes the vulnerability.

questions.q: It is generally sufficient to disable resolution of external entities and disable support for XInclude in order to prevent XXE.
questions.explain: The material states this is generally sufficient, done via parser configuration options or by overriding default behavior.
